extracted.intended_audience: mathematics teachers, lecturers, curriculum designers, and educators (school and university)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for teaching mathematics that emphasizes connections with physics, concrete examples, historically motivated exposition, modeling, and avoidance of purely axiomatic/scholastic pedagogy. Applies to school and university-level mathematics instruction and curriculum design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics as part of physics
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics is a part of physics. Physics is an experimental science, a part of natural science. Mathematics is the part of physics where experiments are cheap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize that mathematical facts (e.g., Jacobi identity) are like experimental facts and should be taught in a way that highlights their connection to physical ideas and experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experiments and concrete examples
rubrics_metrics.description: The Jacobi identity ... is an experimental fact in the same way as that the Earth is round (that is, homeomorphic to a ball). But it can be discovered with less expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach by giving concrete observations and cheap 'experiments' (examples, drawings, computations) that build intuition before abstract formalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid scholastic, cut-off-from-physics mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Since scholastic mathematics that is cut off from physics is fit neither for teaching nor for application in any other science, the result was the universal hate towards mathematicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not present mathematics as isolated axiom-theorem-proof ritual; instead maintain ties to physical intuition and applications to keep it meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivate definitions and constructions by reality/physics
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to understand an unmotivated definition ... Any attempt to do without this interference by physics and reality into mathematics is sectarianism and isolationism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce definitions via natural problems, physical/combinatorial examples, or historical development (e.g., determinant as oriented volume, group as transformations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach modeling and its limits; control deductions by observation
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructing a model, ... certain facts ... are considered to be 'absolutely' correct and are accepted as 'axioms' ... The sense of this 'absoluteness' lies precisely in the fact that we allow ourselves to use these 'facts' according to the rules of formal logic ... The longer and fancier is the chain of deductions ('proofs'), the less reliable is the final result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students that models are idealizations; emphasize the need to test conclusions against examples/observations and be mindful of sensitivity to initial conditions (examples: Malthus equation, weather forecasting, docking maneuvers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer concrete/visual geometric intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawing a curve given by parametric equations ... is a totally impossible problem for students ... Beginning with l’Hospital’s first textbook on calculus ('calculus for understanding of curved lines') ... the ability to solve such problems was considered ... a necessary part of the craft of every mathematician.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include drawing, visualization, and geometric examples (paraboloids, hypocycloids, Riemann surfaces) early in instruction to build intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach important classical results for intuition (not only modern abstractions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The theorem of classification of surfaces is a top-class mathematical achievement ... The theorem of classification of surfaces should have been included in high school mathematics courses ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include major classical theorems (surface classification, Abel theorem, Riemann surfaces, elliptic integrals) for their explanatory power, even if proofs are omitted at lower levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historically and empirically motivated pedagogy (observe → generalize → test)
rubrics_metrics.description: First we consider some objects and make some observations in special cases. Then we try and find the limits of application of our observations, look for counter-examples ... As a result we formulate the empirical discovery ... After this there comes the difficult period of checking as to how reliable are the conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure lessons around concrete observations, searching for counterexamples and formulating conjectures before formal proofs and generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid presenting abstract axioms before examples
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to understand an unmotivated definition but this does not stop the criminal algebraists-axiomatisators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce the motivating examples first; only afterwards present axioms/abstract definitions as summaries of observed properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define algebraic concepts via natural constructions (e.g., group as transformations)
rubrics_metrics.description: We get a totally different situation if we start off not with the group but with the concept of a transformation ... A collection of transformations of a set is called a group if along with any two transformations it contains the result of their consecutive application and an inverse transformation along with every transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historically natural and concrete definitions (transformation viewpoint for groups, determinant as volume, manifold as local graph) to make abstract notions meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present smooth manifolds concretely (submanifolds/graphs)
rubrics_metrics.description: A smooth k-dimensional submanifold of the Euclidean space RN is its subset which in a neighbourhood of its every point is a graph of a smooth mapping of Rk into RN−k ... An 'abstract' smooth manifold is a smooth submanifold of a Euclidean space considered up to a diffeomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the explicit graph/submanifold viewpoint over point-set-axiomatic definitions when introducing manifolds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain determinants and Jacobians via volume interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The determinant of a matrix is an (oriented) volume of the parallelepiped whose edges are its columns. If the students are told this secret ... then the whole theory of determinants becomes a clear chapter ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach determinant/Jacobian as oriented volume to demystify algebraic formulas and motivate properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach practical computational skills and 'craft' (times tables, drawing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawing a curve ... was considered to be ... a necessary part of the craft of every mathematician ... (along with the knowledge of the times table).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure students master basic computations and graphical skills rather than only abstract manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid banishing geometry from curricula
rubrics_metrics.description: Mentally challenged zealots of 'abstract mathematics' threw all the geometry ... out of teaching. ... The return of mathematical teaching at all levels from the scholastic chatter to presenting the important domain of natural science is an especially hot problem for France.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep geometry central in curricula because it links mathematics to reality and physics and builds intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight cross-field connections to inspire students
rubrics_metrics.description: Jacobi noted ... that in it one and the same function controls both the presentations of a whole number as a sum of four squares and the real movement of a pendulum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use striking examples of connections between disparate areas (number theory ↔ dynamics, electricity ↔ magnetism analogies) to motivate learners and show mathematics as discovery of universal patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach detection and use of counterexamples to limit overgeneralization
rubrics_metrics.description: Then we try and find the limits of application of our observations, look for counter-examples which would prevent unjustified extension of our observations onto a too wide range of events (example: the number of partitions ... gives the sequence 1,2,4,8,16, but then comes 29).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to actively search for counterexamples as a method to delimit conjectures and understand hypotheses' necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warn against long, fancy chains of deduction without checks
rubrics_metrics.description: The longer and fancier is the chain of deductions ('proofs'), the less reliable is the final result ... The technology of combatting such errors is the same external control by experiments or observations ... and it should be taught from the very beginning to all juniors in schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize verification via examples and external checks; train students in spotting and controlling errors in long arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simple models; avoid unnecessary complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex models are rarely useful (unless for those writing their dissertations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage using simple, interpretable models in applications and teaching, reserving complex models for well-motivated contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hands-on/combinatorial examples to justify algebraic facts
rubrics_metrics.description: It is only possible to understand the commutativity of multiplication by counting and re-counting soldiers by ranks and files or by calculating the area of a rectangle in the two ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground algebraic properties in counting, geometry, or combinatorial reasoning so students see why axioms hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include classic pedagogical texts and historical sources
rubrics_metrics.description: All the best and most important in methodical approach mathematical books are almost unknown to students here ... Among these are Numbers and figures by Rademacher and Töplitz, Geometry and the imagination by Hilbert and Cohn-Vossen, What is mathematics? by Courant and Robbins, How to solve it and Mathematics and plausible reasoning by Polya, Development of mathematics in the 19th century by F. Klein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend that teachers and curricula draw on classical methodical texts and the tradition of problem-solving and plausible reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach advanced, motivating topics where appropriate (Riemann surfaces, elliptic integrals, Abel theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: ENS students ... turned out be acquainted neither with the Riemann surface of an elliptic curve ... nor with the topological classification of surfaces ... They were only taught Hodge structures and Jacobi varieties!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce students (at suitable levels) to deep motivating topics that reveal structure and connections rather than emphasizing empty abstract formalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stress the social and communicative role of mathematics education
rubrics_metrics.description: If mathematicians do not come to their senses, then the consumers who preserved a need in a modern ... mathematical theory ... will in the end turn down the services of the undereducated scholastics in both the schools and the universities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design teaching so mathematics remains relevant and respected by society and allied sciences; avoid approaches that alienate potential users and students.
